title: 7 Hidden Games Running Your Meetings
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli asks why groups of capable people reach decisions weaker than the sum of their parts, and answers that the cause is interaction dynamics rather than individual skill. She frames this with the group-psychology formula of actual productivity as potential minus process loss plus process gain, then uses game theory as a diagnostic vocabulary for leaders. Seven classic games (Prisoner's Dilemma, Stag Hunt, Battle of the Sexes, Chicken, Tragedy of the Commons, Public Goods, Ultimatum) are each paired with a workplace example such as whistleblowing, system adoption, mergers, salary negotiation and equity splits. The piece then zooms in on the Prisoner's Dilemma to show that the way a leader frames a question changes the payoff of honesty. Her closing move is practical: do not just analyse the game, design it, using learning-framed rather than blame-framed questions.
points: Group outcomes depend on process losses and gains, not just member talent, so leaders should design for coordination and motivation rather than hope for brilliance.
Each classic game maps to a recurring workplace trap, for example the Stag Hunt to cross-department technology adoption and the Public Goods game to under-maintained shared knowledge bases.
In the Prisoner's Dilemma, honest answers are cooperation and safe answers are defection, so candour is rare when honesty feels exposed.
A blame-framed question raises the cost of honesty while a future-oriented, learning-framed one lowers it, so question framing is a lever on team behaviour.
quotes: In other words, success or failure is less about individual brilliance and more about how strategies combine or collide in a collective setting.

Process losses occur when groups perform worse than expected based on the abilities of their individual members. Common sources include poor coordination (members not syncing efforts), motivational issues (social loafing, free-riding) and limited individual capability in group contexts (members holding back due to group pressure or unclear roles).
Game theory gives leaders tools to diagnose how process losses and gains emerge by modelling dynamics that shape whether teams compete, cooperate or unlock their full collective potential.

Innovation adoption in companies often looks like a stag hunt. A new digital system delivers value only if several departments adopt it together. Finance, operations and HR must all commit to switching workflows, training staff, integrating data, etc. If even one department opts out, the promised benefits of integration collapse, and everyone falls back to fragmented, inefficient systems.
Why defect? Because if I answer honestly and others don’t, I’m left exposed. But if everyone defects, we all get worse outcomes: poor insights, bad strategy, wasted time.
A blame-framed question raises the cost of honesty, pushing people to defect. A learning-framed question lowers the cost of honesty, making cooperation (truth-telling) rational.

Questions are levers: they reframe risks and signal whether cooperation is safe. A careless question can trigger defensiveness and push people into zeroIsum behaviour. A thoughtful one can make honesty rational, collaboration attractive and fairness explicit.
